output.headline: Burnham confirms free national care service, funded by ending triple lock
output.bodyHtml:
Andy Burnham has put forward a wide-ranging package of policies on social care, electoral reform and Europe, telling voters that the plan will break the mould of the last 40 years and ‘allow us to rise again’.

In a deeply personal speech at Labour’s conference, Burnham began building his next general election manifesto around that plan, while acknowledging that the sharp new dividing lines he is creating in politics could carry a personal political cost.

‘I won’t pretend some of this won’t be difficult,’ he said. ‘I accept I may pay a political price. But someone has to go through the pain barrier and rip the plaster off.’

The prime minister said he would try to give people some ‘breathing space’ on the cost of living now, though he admitted his ambitious policy prospectus would have to wait until after the next election because of the state of the public finances.

‘These things are not everything, but I hope you will see it as a sign – a strong one – of our intent to get your bills and fares down as you wait for the bigger changes to come,’ he told Labour activists.

‘I would love to go quicker, but I have to be honest about what the country can afford. I will stick to our fiscal rules to get borrowing and debt down. The approach I am outlining today is the responsible one.’

Burnham was determined to leave his audience in the conference hall in Liverpool, and at home, with some hope, even as global economic storm clouds gather and Labour slipped behind Reform UK in one poll this week.

During his hour-long speech, in which he paused several times, overcome with emotion at mentioning the death of his father, Burnham said he wanted to show the UK was ‘something worth saving, worth fighting for’.

He said: ‘I believe the plan I have outlined today will not just hold us together, it will allow us to rise again.

‘Today we draw a line on a decade of division. We stop doomscrolling on posts running Britain down. And we put the country on a new path.’

Burnham promised to be unflinchingly honest with the public about where, in his view, the country had gone wrong, saying it was time to admit ‘Brexit hasn’t given us control’ and that it was a handbrake on growth.

Burnham gave his strongest hint yet that he would look again at the UK’s membership of the EU, saying he would set out plans for a longer-term relationship with the bloc at the reset summit this autumn.

Options could include trading relationships along the lines that Norway, Switzerland or Canada have with the EU, the customs union or single market, or even reversing Brexit in its entirety.

‘We will not give Britain the clear path we need into the rest of this century until we decide on a long-term relationship with what is still our largest market,’ he said. ‘I cannot say to you truthfully that where we are is good enough. Brexit has done more harm than good. We need to restore a high level of growth and prosperity for Britain.’

Public attitudes towards leaving the EU have shifted over time, though Burnham’s shift away from Keir Starmer’s manifesto red lines will still be a big political gamble in seats such as his own, Makerfield, which voted for Brexit.

Burnham confirmed he would end the pensions triple lock should Labour win the next election, using the savings to fund a national care service in England that would be free at the point of use.

He plans to break the link between wage growth and pensions and promised instead a rise based on inflation or 2.5 per cent, whichever is higher, which he claimed would still leave millions of pensioners better off.

He said pensioners would benefit from the new care system – which would be expected to follow the Scottish system in covering care costs but not accommodation – and a promise to exempt them from income tax.

Burnham suggested that care workers were ‘invisible to the political class’ but he told them: ‘You are not invisible to me. I see you. I thank you. And I am sorry that my profession has let down yours for so long.’

As well as a promise to fix the broken system, the prime minister’s words will be interpreted as a sign he is preparing to carve out migrant care workers from Shabana Mahmood’s immigration measures.

In another commitment to a long-held belief, Burnham also confirmed he would put electoral reform in Labour’s next manifesto, announcing a cross-party national commission to consider options to replace first past the post with a form of proportional representation.

‘We can’t succeed in the eyes of the world if we continue with the levels of political turbulence we have seen in recent times,’ he said. ‘It is always in my mind that I’m the seventh prime minister in 10 years. It is why I want to underpin our plan for Britain with a new politics.

Related: Conference laps up Andy unplugged as he offers chance to take road less travelled | John Crace

‘We will all have failed in our public duties if we carry on as we are and open the door of No 10 to a divisive government on 30 per cent of the vote or less.’

Burnham said it was the drive of his government for every person to feel greater control over the basics of life and renew faith that systems could work for them.

He said the common wealth of Britain, its homes, energy, water and care, had been stripped out and sold for profit. ‘The wealth we had created for the many was seen as an opportunity for the few,’ he said.

‘The British right talk about taking back control. Never let them forget, they are the ones that gave it away in the first place,’ he said in remarks that drew a standing ovation.

Burnham promised two new pieces of legislation later this year, including a leasehold reform bill that would put curbs on charges for homes.

‘The days of you being squeezed for every penny are coming to an end,’ he said. ‘This is the break we are making with the flawed thinking of the last 40 years. Not seeing housing only as a market with winners and losers, but as an essential everyone needs for a good life.’

He said a water bill would repeal Margaret Thatcher’s ban on state-owned water companies, which was a ‘symbol of what had gone wrong with Britain’. There will be new curbs on bosses and pay and new powers for mayors over water systems.

He also confirmed the creation of GB Grid, which will use money previously allocated to Great British Energy to compete with privately owned companies such as National Grid, while ministers will speed up the breaking of the link between energy prices and the international gas market.

The Tory leader, Kemi Badenoch, said: ‘Burnham wants to take Britain back to the 1970s – a time of more government control, more trade union control and no economic growth. There is a reason our country took a different course after that decade.

‘Nothing Burnham announced today will do anything to fix Britain’s long-term problems. He had no plan to fix our stagnant economy. No plan to fund defence. No plan to sort out the spiralling welfare bill beyond more government schemes.’

Reform UK’s Nigel Farage said: ‘By potentially scrapping the triple lock, Andy Burnham will abdicate his responsibility to British pensioners. Instead of cutting our bloated benefits bill, stopping migrants from accessing benefits, or slashing foreign aid, he’s considering launching an offensive against our elderly.’

Labour MPs responded with relief and enthusiasm to Burnham’s conference address, which the prime minister wrote almost entirely alone, with more than one describing it as the speech of their political lifetimes.

There were also words of caution from some ministers and Downing Street insiders, who will be more interested in how the speech goes down with the wider public at home than in the room.

‘I don’t want to be negative, but we’ve got to be realistic,’ one cabinet minister said. ‘We just don’t know what’s going to happen with the economic headwinds. But if anybody can get us through it, Andy can.’
output.standfirst:
The prime minister has confirmed plans for a free national care service, funded by ending the pensions triple lock, alongside reforms – but he admits it will be difficult and he may pay a political price.

  • Analysis: PM’s promises will take time to come good

  • Key takeaways from Burnham’s conference speech
output.progress: The government is setting up a cross-party commission to explore replacing first-past-the-post with proportional representation.

output.headline: New alert system keeps Ukrainian businesses open through drone raids
output.bodyHtml:
A new two-tier alert system is helping more than half of Ukraine’s businesses keep working through Russian drone alerts, according to the country’s economy minister, even as missile alerts are costing Ukraine an estimated $45m (£34m) for every hour they bring business to a halt, as Kyiv searches for ways to keep the economy running under an intensifying Russian bombardment.

Russia has increasingly targeted the infrastructure underpinning Ukraine’s economy, striking industrial sites, warehouses, logistics hubs and datacentres in what Oleksandr Kravchenko, the minister for economy and the environment, described as an effort to “destroy pretty much the entire economy”.

“What we had not fully anticipated was how quickly Russia would develop these jet-powered drones and use them to target everything,” he said, referring to Russia’s use of the new weapons that have pounded Kyiv in recent weeks.

Speaking from the heavily protected government building in Kyiv, Kravchenko, a former McKinsey executive who joined the government in the summer, said the attacks were forcing large parts of the economy into repeated standstills as workers were sent to shelters, with sirens lasting up to 10 hours a day.

“If people are in a bunker, business stops,” he said.

The government recently introduced a new two-tier warning system designed to keep businesses operating during prolonged air raid alerts, easing some of the economic costs.

A “red” alert warns of a missile threat and requires people to seek shelter, while a “yellow” warning is used for drone threats, allowing many businesses to remain open.

Kravchenko said more than half of businesses were continuing to operate during yellow alerts.

But a yellow alert is no guarantee of safety. That danger was made clear on Monday, when a Russian jet-powered drone struck the National Academy of Sciences in central Kyiv during a yellow alert, killing two people while staff were still inside working.

It is one of the difficult trade-offs Ukraine faces as it tries to keep normal life moving while protecting people from an escalating campaign of Russian strikes.

Kravchenko said Russian attacks this year alone had caused an estimated $10bn in damage to fixed assets, with steel plants, warehouses, logistics infrastructure and, most recently datacentres, among the targets. Russia has also effectively blockaded Ukraine’s Black Sea ports, which before the blockade carried the bulk of the country’s exports.

The minister believed the government was better prepared this year for what could be the “hardest, the harshest winter” of the war, with further pressure expected on energy supplies, infrastructure and businesses already weakened by months of strikes.

The government is now discussing ways to allow more private companies to purchase Ukraine’s air-defence system to protect against future strikes, the minister said, although he cautioned that businesses could never fully protect themselves from Russian missiles and drones.

The ongoing damage from strikes has added to an already severe strain on the state’s finances.

Despite the EU having already agreed a €90bn loan package for Ukraine covering 2026 and 2027, the president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has recently put Ukraine’s remaining budget shortfall this year at about $27bn, a figure that has prompted questions among some European governments over how the gap emerged.

Kravchenko said the government had since narrowed the shortfall to $20bn through spending cuts and by identifying additional domestic reserves.

Kravchenko said Kyiv was now seeking further support from the EU, Japan, Canada and the UK, including potentially bringing forward loans that had been earmarked for next year.

“There is very active work with all our international partners to get additional sources of funding,” he said.

Kravchenko dismissed suggestions that the shortfall was the result of mismanagement or corruption. He also said it was not due to excessive spending under former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov, whose drive to overhaul military procurement and rapidly expand Ukraine’s drone programme had made him one of the government’s most prominent reformers before his dismissal in July, a move that triggered street protests.

Instead, he said the gap reflected both weaker-than-expected state revenues and the rising cost of waging the war.

“The cost of war is simply increasing,” he said, pointing to the need for more air-defence systems and for Ukraine to accelerate development of drones capable of intercepting Russia’s new jet-powered weapons.

But high-profile corruption scandals have also reached Zelenskyy’s inner circle, straining trust in the government both at home and among western donors.

A recent poll by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology found that corruption in government was the most cited concern among Ukrainians, named by 50 per cent of respondents, ahead of mass missile and drone strikes at 40 per cent. The same survey found that 72 per cent believed Zelenskyy bore personal responsibility for corrupt actions by people around him.

Kravchenko said progress had been made to tackle the issue but said Ukraine still faced both corruption itself and a persistent perception problem both inside Ukraine and abroad.

“I very much appreciate the pressure of European partners on reforms,” he said, adding that Ukraine also needed to tackle perceptions of corruption at home and abroad.

The minister said Ukraine’s external financing needs for 2027 are estimated at $52.6bn, but only about $20bn has so far been secured, with further tax rises and spending cuts under discussion.

Asked whether the rise of parties sceptical of support for Ukraine in France and Germany could weaken western commitment to Kyiv, he said: “Am I worried? I think I should be, probably.”

“The overall fatigue is increasing in Europe,” he added.
output.standfirst: A two-tier alert system now lets more than half of Ukraine’s businesses keep working through drone alerts, as missile threats cost an estimated $45m for every hour they force a halt, the economy minister says.
output.progress: Ukraine’s government introduced a two-tier alert system that lets more than half of businesses keep operating during drone warnings.

output.headline: Residents return home as investigation finds no explosives near RAF Fairford
output.bodyHtml:
A forensic examination of the vans found no explosives, the head of Britain’s counter-terrorism police has said, days after five men were arrested near RAF Fairford over a suspected Iran-backed plot. Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor said: ‘Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found. However, a quantity of petrol was recovered.’

Police bailed the men on Monday after examining what was found in the vans and searching addresses linked to them across London, all of which found no evidence of a viable device. The suspects had first been arrested on explosives charges, then later for preparing acts of terrorism.

One of the five men called the police himself to report the incident, it has emerged.

The call from the man, who is in his 20s and from London, was one reason armed police were scrambled to arrest the group, who were with three vans close to the military base the US has used in its attacks on Iran.

Police first on the scene found several barrels in the vans, one of which contained petrol, while the others were empty, the Guardian understands.

By Tuesday, residents were returning home after spending days evacuated from their village.

An Iranian link to the weekend’s events in the Gloucestershire countryside is seen as increasingly likely, as the police and security services investigation continues. Senior US politicians, including President Donald Trump, have said they were surprised that the suspects were released on bail.

A farmer driving home from a party at around 1am on Sunday had spotted the men and vans and called 999, it was revealed on Sunday. Why one of the suspects also called police remains another strand of the complex investigation.

The Times first reported the news of the call to police by one of the suspects.

Assistant commissioner Laurence Taylor set out several reasons officers swooped on the rural location in an earlier statement. He said: ‘A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford.’

The mounting view among investigators that Iran was involved led Andy Burnham to call a meeting of Cobra, the government’s crisis committee, on Monday, which senior police and security officials attended.

Ministers have been briefed that Iran has various reasons for hiring proxies, who are sometimes unwitting, to carry out acts that aim to eat up resources and create chaos.

Counter-terrorism police are leading the investigation, working to establish why the five men, all British nationals from London, were in the Gloucestershire countryside, close to a sensitive site, in the dead of night.

The vans were marked with the logo of a legitimate fuel transit company, which later denied owning the vehicles.

Taylor defended the decision to bail the suspects, saying: ‘Yesterday we released the five men on police bail. They remain under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions while we continue our work. The safety of the public is at the forefront of our investigative decision-making, and this was certainly the case yesterday.

‘I understand why this development will have come as a surprise to many, but I’d like to reiterate that it was an investigative decision, and one which is grounded in experience and careful consideration of policing powers.’

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, said the events were the work of a ‘foreign actor’ but did not give further details. He said ‘a lot of people are disturbed’ after the suspects’ release from custody, while Trump had earlier said he was ‘surprised’ the group had been freed.

Speculation has been growing about a connection between the weekend’s incident and Iran. Taylor said on Monday that he knew there was ‘significant interest in whether the current geopolitical context has a bearing on this incident’.

He added: ‘But be assured, we are considering this from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals either knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state.’

In March, the British government gave the US permission to use the base for ‘specific defensive operations into Iran’.

The Iranian embassy in London has said it ‘categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations’ of Iranian involvement.

Eighty-five households were forced to decamp to a leisure centre on Sunday as the bomb squad and counter-terror police descended on the village of Whelford, where the men were arrested.

Some of the evacuated residents were able to stay with family, about 60 people received support from a Cotswold district council rest centre in Cirencester, and 28 people were accommodated overnight in hotels.

Father Michael Robertson, the priest at the nearby St Thomas Catholic church, told PA: ‘A lot of parishioners didn’t think they could get to church. Those that came were worried but perfectly happy with the situation.

‘In fact, quite a lot of Americans who have deployed here actually come to mass and some of the permanently deployed Americans are full members of the parish. We’re quite contented with the situation generally. Obviously, the disruption upsets people.’

Additional reporting by Jamie Grierson
output.standfirst: Forensic tests found no explosives in the vans, but the case remains a live inquiry into a suspected Iran-backed plot after five men were arrested near RAF Fairford, and US politicians have questioned their bail.
output.progress: Counter-terrorism police say forensic tests found no explosives in the vans, and evacuated residents have returned home.

output.headline: Supreme court lets deportations to third countries resume without a hearing
output.bodyHtml:
The Trump administration can resume quickly deporting immigrants to ‘third countries’ – or countries other than their homeland – without giving them any opportunity to contest their removals, the supreme court ruled on Tuesday.

The six-justice conservative majority of the high court temporarily lifted a lower-court decision that required the administration to give immigrants sufficient notice and the opportunity to claim fear of torture or persecution in the countries where they are being sent – a stipulation the Trump administration said had prevented it from ‘efficiently removing aliens’ from the US.

Related: Gone in 90 seconds: an ‘invisibilized’ ICE is arresting more people than ever

As is typical in emergency orders, the justices did not explain why they granted the administration’s request.

The three liberal justices of the court, Sonia Sotomayor, Elena Kagan and Ketanji Brown Jackson, dissented from the order.

Tuesday’s ruling will take effect while the supreme court considers the larger question in the case. Justices said they would hear oral arguments in December.

It is the second time the supreme court has sided with the Trump administration over ‘third-country’ deportations.

Todd Blanche, the attorney general, called the administration’s policies ‘entirely lawful and a critical tool for immigration enforcement’ in a social media post following the supreme court’s order.

‘Unlike the lower court, SCOTUS waited to hear from both sides before making the decision,’ Blanche wrote.

The supreme court’s intervention comes days after the administration filed an emergency request to the justices, hoping to continue deporting immigrants to third countries – including those that the US state department considers dangerous.

The Trump administration has entered into a series of agreements with other countries that have allowed it to deport more than 25,000 immigrants to at least 29 countries, according to Third Country Deportation Watch, a project run by Refugees International and Human Rights First.

Countries that have received US deportees include the Central African Republic, which is grappling with unrest and terrorism due to political and militia instability, and South Sudan, where a humanitarian emergency has been unfolding because of political and economic disintegration.

On Monday, two dozen UN human rights experts cautioned that the deportation of thousands of migrants from the US to third countries has set off a ‘cascade of human rights violations’ that could have ‘deadly’ consequences.

Many third-country deportees have faced dire conditions and violence after they ended up in countries without any legal status. Earlier this month, two men whom the Trump administration expelled to Equatorial Guinea were bound, fitted with bags over their heads, beaten and pushed down a flight of stairs, all in plain view of other US deportees, according to witnesses and human rights lawyers. Detainees said the men were facing retaliation for speaking to journalists and human rights experts about the poor conditions they faced.

‘This cruel and inhumane policy is a black eye on Lady Liberty,’ said Adelita Grijalva, a Democratic representative from Arizona. ‘We are a nation that promises to welcome the “poor” and “huddled masses” yearning for freedom. Instead, we are sending vulnerable people into harm’s way – and, in some cases, potentially to their deaths.’

One of the men who was beaten in Equatorial Guinea was her constituent, Ahmed Soliman – a gay man from Egypt who had fled discrimination in his home country and spent most of his life in Phoenix.

Lawyers for the immigrants have challenged the ‘third country’ deportation policy, arguing that they had not been given ‘notice and a meaningful opportunity to present fear-based claims’.

Lawyers for the administration have said there’s no need for individual fear-based claims because countries willing to accept immigrants have already agreed not to persecute or torture anyone. The solicitor general, D John Sauer, the government’s attorney, wrote to the supreme court that the lower-court orders ‘created substantial logistical problems with ongoing removal operations – including the cancellation of flights – and led to added expense, potential diplomatic issues, and the inability to remove dangerous criminals’.

Prior to the supreme court’s order on Tuesday, two lower courts had separately sided with the immigrants.
output.standfirst: The conservative-majority court lifted a lower-court order requiring notice before removal, with three justices dissenting, as UN experts caution the policy has set off a 'cascade of human rights violations' that could have 'deadly' consequences.

output.headline: Commission’s verdict vindicates Premier League’s pursuit of Manchester City case, says Masters
output.bodyHtml:
The Premier League has hailed an independent commission’s decision to find Manchester City guilty of all charges of breaching its financial rules over a nine-year period as vindication of its pursuit of the case, after the club was found to have boosted its income by more than £900m.

Masters said: ‘The core decision establishes the facts of what happened at Manchester City during this period. It details how the club systematically broke Premier League rules for nearly a decade. It also vindicates the Premier League’s decision to pursue this case against Manchester City.’

He said, in relation to sanctions: ‘Now we have the commission’s decision, we are committed to moving swiftly through the remainder of the process, to provide certainty for the league, our clubs and fans.’

The Premier League said the independent commission had found City guilty of arranging ‘sham’ contracts with commercial partners to inflate revenues artificially and reduce costs, and of filing inaccurate accounts that concealed the true state of its finances – which, correctly reported, would have shown significant breaches of Premier League and Uefa spending limits.

Related: Manchester City’s ‘sham’ seasons: how they fared and who was in charge

The commission also found the club had entered into ‘sham’ image rights deals with players and the then manager, Roberto Mancini, to inflate their earnings artificially.

City said they will appeal by Friday’s deadline ‘on the basis that the opinion contains clear material errors, of law, principle and fact, and is unsafe’. Their chief executive, Ferran Soriano, said in a video sent to employees that the decision was based on a ‘Premier League conspiracy theory’.

The appeal is expected to run alongside a sanctions hearing presided over by the independent commission, with the Premier League keen to conclude matters as quickly as possible.

The scale of what Hull’s owner, Acun Ilicali, has called City’s ‘financial doping’ has sent shock waves through football, leaving executives at other Premier League clubs taken aback.

The Premier League’s chief executive, Richard Masters, described the case as ‘the most significant in Premier League history’. It seems inevitable that this will lead to a punishment with no precedent, including in all probability a points deduction that would condemn City to relegation.

There is no direct precedent given the scale of City’s offences, though Everton’s 10-point penalty for breaching profitability and sustainability rules by £19.5m, in a case ending with the 2021-22 season, was based on a Premier League tariff of six points for the initial breach plus a further point for every £5m overspent.

The commission was critical of the behaviour of City’s witnesses during the hearings. ‘Evidence given by a number of important factual witnesses called to give evidence on behalf of the club was false in a number of key respects’, it wrote, adding that some witnesses had given evidence ‘they knew to be untrue and so had been dishonest’.

The commission found City had operated a ‘disguised funding scheme’ worth £830.6m over nine seasons, from 2009-10 to 2017-18, and had hidden costs by a further £70m. It also found the club guilty of multiple breaches of failing to cooperate with the Premier League and act in good faith, concluding that City had made concerted efforts to stop and frustrate the investigation.

The Premier League published a redacted 40-page ‘core decision’ from the independent commission, which took almost two years to produce after a 42-day hearing that concluded in December 2024.

The league said: ‘The independent commission found City arranged “sham” commercial deals with a number of its sponsors during the period, which were part of a disguised funding scheme, whereby those companies were only required to pay a portion of the relevant sponsorship fees. The remainder was funded by Abu Dhabi United Group Investment & Development Ltd (ADUG), which owned the club.

‘As part of the scheme, further “sham” arrangements, funded by ADUG, were entered into to enable the club to record lower operating expenses than it actually incurred, as well as a “sham” circular arrangement with Fordham, an entity that purchased the club’s players’ image rights, that was funded by ADUG.

‘The purpose of these schemes was found to have been to inflate the club’s revenues artificially, and reduce its costs, by more than £900m during the affected period, to appear to comply with financial rules.

‘The consequence of this, as the commission found, was that the club filed misstated accounts and concealed the true state of its finances from its auditors and football regulators.’

ADUG bought City on behalf of Sheikh Mansour bin Zayed al-Nahyan for £200m in 2008, and the new owners made an immediate impact by paying £32.5m to sign the Brazilian superstar Robinho from Real Madrid. That began a spending spree City struggled to afford from their existing revenues, and the independent commission concluded that the only way to match the owners’ ambitions for the club was for ADUG to ‘provide very significant funds by way of equity contribution’.

The commission’s report states that in 2010 City devised a scheme whereby sponsors would pay a ‘base sum’ and ADUG would pay a ‘tagged sum’, even though the base sum was the only true revenue; the recorded sponsorship fee was the total of the two.

City’s lawyers argued that the ‘tagged sum’ was a loan by the Abu Dhabi government against liabilities on sponsorship fees, but the commission rejected that argument.

Related: Manchester City CEO Soriano says guilty verdicts are ‘a Premier League conspiracy theory’

The judgment is a significant win for the Premier League and Masters. Although the commission found that City breached Uefa’s spending limits, there appears little prospect of Uefa’s case being revisited, as a five-year statute of limitations applies to its disciplinary proceedings; Uefa’s punishment of City over alleged financial fair play breaches was largely overturned in 2020 by the court of arbitration for sport, which found ‘most of the alleged breaches were either not established or time-barred’.

Other Premier League clubs are surprised City have not reached an agreed sanction with the Premier League, given the judgment, but City continue to deny wrongdoing. ‘Manchester City FC is both disappointed and surprised by the opinion of the Premier League commission, that has been published today,’ the club said. ‘The club is innocent of the accusations made by the Premier League and a comprehensive body of irrefutable evidence exists in support of all of its positions, relating to this case. The club will therefore be relentless, and where necessary proactive, in any and all appropriate regulatory and legal forums.’
output.standfirst:
• Richard Masters says the commission’s verdict vindicates the Premier League’s pursuit of what he calls its most significant case

  • Independent commission finds City guilty of breaching financial rules over nine seasons, inflating income by more than £900m through ‘sham’ contracts; club will appeal before Friday’s deadline
output.progress: The Premier League says it is committed to moving swiftly through the sanctions process to give clubs and fans certainty.

output.headline: Largest trial yet finds retatrutide drives major weight reduction and health gains
output.bodyHtml:
The ‘Godzilla’ of weight-loss drugs could help improve blood sugar levels, reduce inflammation and cut a person’s body weight by a quarter, according to the largest study of its kind.

Retatrutide mimics three key gut hormones that help control appetite, blood sugar and metabolism: GLP-1, GIP and glucagon. Unlike other drugs such as Wegovy, which primarily targets the GLP-1 pathway to suppress appetite, or Mounjaro, which contains GLP-1 plus GIP to control blood sugar levels, retatrutide also engages the glucagon receptor, which helps increase energy expenditure.

The results of the global trial in people living with obesity and type 2 diabetes suggest retatrutide could help them shift enormous amounts of excess weight while also providing other important health benefits, though the drug has not yet been approved by any regulatory agency.

‘Retatrutide demonstrated substantial reduction in body weight alongside glycaemic control and cardiometabolic risk factors, with a safety profile generally similar to other molecules with GLP-1 receptor agonist activity,’ the researchers said.

Related: Does GLP-1 use result in significant hair loss?

The findings from the study, funded by retatrutide maker Eli Lilly, were published in the Lancet medical journal and presented at the annual meeting of the European Association for the Study of Diabetes in Milan, Italy.

The randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial enrolled 2,047 adults in eight countries: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, India, Mexico, Romania, Spain and the US.

Participants had a body mass index (BMI) of 27 or above and type 2 diabetes. 48 per cent were women and 52 per cent were men. Their average age was 55.

In the 80-week phase 3 trial, 1,152 were randomly assigned to receive a weekly injection of placebo (289), or retatrutide 4 mg (292), 9 mg (284) or 12 mg (287), alongside dietary counselling and guidance on physical activity.

By the end of the study, those on 4 mg of retatrutide lost 11.9 per cent of their body weight on average, increasing to 16.8 per cent with 9 mg and 18.8 per cent on 12 mg. Those in the placebo group lost 5.1 per cent.

Among those on the 12 mg dose, almost half (47 per cent) shed at least 20 per cent of their starting weight and almost a third (31 per cent) lost at least 25 per cent. That compared with 6 per cent and 3 per cent, respectively, with placebo.

Additionally, 72 per cent achieved an HbA1c (measuring average blood sugar levels for the last two to three months) of 6.5 per cent or lower, a standard threshold used to diagnose type 2 diabetes, compared with 29 per cent in the placebo group.

Retatrutide also significantly improved cardiometabolic risk factors, including blood pressure and lipid profiles, and reduced high-sensitivity C-reactive protein (hsCRP), a marker of inflammation, according to the researchers.

Related: ‘It’s problematic’: concern as weight-loss jab maker sponsors Vogue World event

The most frequently reported adverse events were gastrointestinal. Diarrhoea occurred in 27-34 per cent of participants in the retatrutide groups, compared with 13 per cent in the placebo group, and nausea occurred in 14-28 per cent of participants on retatrutide, compared with 8 per cent receiving the placebo.

Seven deaths occurred during the trial: two in the retatrutide 4 mg group, three in the 9 mg group, one in the 12 mg group and one in the placebo group, and were deemed unrelated to the study intervention by the investigator.

Meanwhile, separate research presented at the conference in Milan and published in the Lancet Obstetrics, Gynaecology & Women’s Health medical journal showed that in most cases, weight-loss drugs are not associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes in women living with type 2 diabetes.

But researchers stressed that more research was urgently needed to address the large evidence gaps and to keep pace with the huge and accelerating rise in women of reproductive age using the drugs.
output.standfirst: In the largest study, retatrutide cut body weight by up to 18.8 per cent and improved blood sugar and inflammation, though it is not yet approved by regulators and caused more diarrhoea and nausea.
output.progress: Researchers behind the Eli Lilly-funded trial say retatrutide cut body weight by up to 18.8 per cent while improving blood sugar control and reducing inflammation.

output.headline: Little terns achieve record breeding season, National Trust says
output.bodyHtml:
New figures from the National Trust reveal signs of recovery at England’s most important tern colonies, which have been hit by years of bird flu, flooding and increasingly unpredictable weather.

The trust reported record numbers of little terns at Long Nanny in Northumberland, one of the UK’s most important breeding sites for what is the country’s second-rarest breeding seabird.

Numbers are also slightly up for arctic terns, the long-distance superstars of the avian world that annually breed in places such as Northumberland before making the incredible journey south to Antarctica.

More than 1,100 pairs of sandwich terns returned to breed at Blakeney Point in Norfolk after a two-year absence.

Ben McCarthy, the trust’s head of nature conservation, stressed there was no room for complacency.

But he said the figures showed “what can be achieved when internationally important breeding sites are carefully protected and managed.

“These results are particularly encouraging given the challenges seabirds have faced in recent years – from avian flu and extreme weather to wider pressures on the marine environment.”

The trust said there had been a “remarkable turnaround” for little terns at Long Nanny, with at least 126 pairs nesting – doubling the previous site record.

At least 82 chicks are known to have fledged, with the final total potentially exceeding 100 birds, rangers said.

Little terns are a particularly sensitive and vulnerable species that migrate from west Africa to breed, making nests, known as scrapes, on open sandy beaches.

The species had experienced “significant long-term declines nationally, making this year’s record breeding season especially significant”, the trust said.

The arctic tern colony at Long Nanny consisted of at least 730 breeding pairs this year, with nests containing 1,346 eggs – slightly up, and a sign of numbers “holding steady” after a torrid few years for the species.

In 2023, Long Nanny’s arctic tern colony was devastated by avian flu, when rangers found more than 600 dead chicks. In recent seasons nests have also been lost to high spring tides and extreme weather, the trust said.

James Porteus, the trust’s lead ranger for the Northumberland coast, said it was “incredibly encouraging” to see little terns doing so well, calling it an “exceptional season” after several years “dominated by bird flu outbreaks, flooded nests and concerns about declining numbers”.

Related: Skylarks and sandwich terns among new birdies on reserve created from ‘boring old golf course’

He added: “To more than double the previous site record for breeding pairs is a remarkable achievement and a testament to the dedication of staff, volunteers and partner organisations who help protect the colony each year.

“It’s especially exciting to see so many chicks hatching and fledging. Little terns face huge challenges throughout their migration and breeding cycle, so every successful nesting attempt matters.”

Rangers in Northumberland also reported the return, for the seventh consecutive breeding season, of a black tern they have called Nigella. Black terns are not normally found breeding in the UK.

The trust stressed that the picture for breeding seabirds was “not universally positive”, pointing to a 27 per cent fall in arctic tern numbers on the Farne Islands, Northumberland. There were also no common terns there this year, compared with five last year, while sandwich tern numbers remained unchanged at two breeding pairs.

output.headline: Scientists set out to explain Antarctica’s changing winter sea ice
output.bodyHtml:
Scientists have confirmed, using decades of satellite monitoring, that Antarctica’s winter sea ice has peaked at its third-lowest level on record, falling a million square kilometres – or almost 400,000 square miles – short of the long-term average.

The confirmation meant the four lowest years on record for the continent’s sea ice – a vital component of the planet’s climate and critical for marine life – have now all occurred in the past four years.

Satellites have been tracking the continent’s sea ice since 1979, and this year’s data showed it peaked on 14 September at 17.59m square kilometres, about a million square kilometres short of the average maximum, an area roughly twice the size of Spain.

Dr Walt Meier, a senior scientist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center at the University of Colorado, said the centre had held off declaring the maximum because there was a ‘lot of potential variability’ at this stage in the continent’s sea ice cycle.

But he said sea ice levels had been falling since 14 September, and he now thought ‘the maximum has been reached’.

Antarctica’s sea ice goes through an enormous annual swing, melting through summer to below 2m sq km in recent Februaries before growing through winter to above 17m sq km in September.

Recent years, though, have seen records broken for low sea ice in both winter and summer, raising concerns that global heating could be driving the losses.

‘The past four winters have had the lowest sea ice maximum on record – that’s a very clear indication of a system that has changed,’ said Dr Ariaan Purich, a Southern Ocean expert at Monash University in Melbourne.

‘This is not a one-off event any more. The sea ice is no longer covering the same extent of ocean that it used to. We are seeing low winter after low winter and that suggests the sea ice is behaving differently because we have warmed our climate.

This is not a future problem. It’s a now problem.’

Scientists pointed to a France-sized area of open ocean where ice should have been, after a June heatwave pushed temperatures on the Antarctic peninsula to 20C above normal.

In early August, when sea ice should have been steadily expanding, a large area of the Amundsen Sea to the south of the Pacific lost ice instead.

Purich said changes in winds associated with the El Niño climate pattern in the tropical Pacific had likely played a role in reducing the sea ice in that region.

Dr Phil Reid, who monitors Antarctic conditions at Australia’s Bureau of Meteorology, said El Niño tended to change the movement of storm systems around Antarctica, leading some to be held in the same place, churning up the sea ice below.

But he said even without an El Niño, ‘I think we would still be in a similar position … and that is a bit disconcerting’.

‘The atmosphere will play around a bit, but in the end thermodynamics wins. If the water is too warm, you won’t have as much sea ice.’

Purich said that as Antarctica now emerges from its ‘polar night’, sea ice reflects the sun’s energy during the day. But less sea ice meant the Southern Ocean could take up more heat.

Loss of sea ice does not directly affect sea levels, as it was already floating, but it can expose ice shelves to buffeting ocean extremes and weaken them.

Ice shelves slow down the advance of glaciers and the continent’s vast ice sheet, which has the potential to push up global sea levels by many metres if it reaches the ocean.

As well as providing habitats for algae and krill – critical elements of the continent’s food web – unstable sea ice has raised concerns for other species, including emperor penguins, that use the ice to breed and raise young.

Dr Will Hobbs, Antarctic sea ice expert at the University of Tasmania, said Antarctic sea ice had been dropping ‘faster than usual’ since reaching its peak earlier this month.

‘We could be looking at another low summer and that’s when things get really worrying,’ he said, pointing to concerns about impacts on ice shelves.

‘How sensitive is the global climate system to this loss of sea ice? We are still working to put numbers on that. But the system is changing faster than we are understanding it.’
output.standfirst: Scientists are using decades of satellite data and investigating El Niño’s role to explain Antarctica’s third-lowest winter sea ice, a million square kilometres short of the long-term average, with global heating likely a driver.
output.progress: Scientists are investigating what is driving Antarctica’s record-low winter sea ice, including a possible link to El Niño.
